clinicalPearls: A rare non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic arteriopathy defined by lysis of the arterial media, characteristically the outer media adjacent to the adventitia.
It has a strong predilection for splanchnic arteries (coeliac, superior mesenteric, hepatic and splenic) and sometimes involves renal, coronary and intracranial vessels.
Typically presents in middle-aged and older adults with intra-abdominal haemorrhage ('abdominal apoplexy'), dissection, or ruptured aneurysm.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, made only once vasculitis, fibromuscular dysplasia, connective tissue disease and infection have been excluded.
Inflammatory markers and vasculitis serology are characteristically normal, which helps distinguish it from an arteritis.
Angiography reveals a mixture of aneurysms, dissections, stenoses and occlusions, sometimes overlapping with the appearances of fibromuscular dysplasia.
Many authorities regard it as an acute lesion within, or a precursor to, the fibromuscular dysplasia spectrum.
If the patient survives the acute event, the medial lesion may stabilise and heal by reparative fibrosis, occasionally leaving residual stenosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Segmental arterial mediolysis is characterised by vacuolar degeneration and lysis of the smooth muscle of the arterial media, predominantly affecting the outer media near the medioadventitial junction, in the absence of inflammation or atherosclerosis. Loss of this medial support weakens the wall and allows separation at the medioadventitial plane, producing gaps in the arterial wall, dissecting haematomas, pseudoaneurysms and true aneurysms that are prone to rupture and haemorrhage. Alternatively, reparative fibrosis of the damaged segment may cause stenosis or occlusion and downstream ischaemia. The aetiology is unknown, with proposed contributions from vasospasm and catecholamine-mediated arterial injury. There is a striking predilection for the splanchnic circulation, especially the coeliac, mesenteric, hepatic and splenic arteries, with less frequent renal, coronary and intracranial involvement. The condition is increasingly considered to lie on a pathological continuum with fibromuscular dysplasia, potentially representing its acute phase.
additionalDifferentials: Polyarteritis nodosa and other systemic vasculitides
Connective tissue disorders (vascular Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes)
Spontaneous coronary or visceral artery dissection
additionalInvestigations: CT angiography to demonstrate aneurysms, dissection and active haemorrhage
Catheter digital subtraction angiography for detailed vascular mapping and possible intervention
Inflammatory markers and an autoimmune and vasculitis screen to exclude an arteritis
Blood cultures to exclude a mycotic aneurysm
Genetic and connective tissue disorder evaluation where clinically suspected
Histopathology of a resected or biopsied vessel, where medial lysis without inflammation is definitive
Interval MR or CT angiography for surveillance of new or evolving lesions
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability or haemorrhagic shock from a ruptured aneurysm
Acute severe abdominal or flank pain
Features of bowel or solid-organ ischaemia
A rapidly enlarging aneurysm on serial imaging
reference.prognosis: The course is variable and can be life-threatening when acute aneurysm rupture causes major haemorrhage, but the medial lesion may stabilise and heal if the patient survives the acute event. Recurrence and involvement of new arterial territories can occur, so imaging surveillance is advised.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as a vasculitis and giving inappropriate immunosuppression.
Failing to consider it in unexplained spontaneous intra-abdominal haemorrhage.
Overlooking an underlying connective tissue disorder or a mycotic aneurysm.
Assuming a solitary lesion when multifocal, multiterritory disease is common.
Under-recognising the need for ongoing surveillance after the acute presentation.
management: Treat acute aneurysm rupture or active haemorrhage with endovascular intervention (coil embolisation or covered stent) or surgical repair, alongside haemodynamic resuscitation
Control blood pressure to reduce wall stress on affected arteries
Manage stable, unruptured lesions conservatively with close observation given the potential for spontaneous healing
Exclude vasculitis, fibromuscular dysplasia, connective tissue disease and infection before settling on the diagnosis
Involve vascular medicine and interventional radiology in a multidisciplinary approach
Undertake interval imaging surveillance for new aneurysms, dissection or involvement of further arterial territories
